name.text: 01 Content: The Third Tier: Prompting Neural Models for Grammar

questiontext.text:
The Third Tier: Prompting Neural Models for Grammar

Welcome to the final stage of Week Eight. On Tuesday, you parsed and lemmatized twenty words by hand using scholarly dictionaries. That manual work gave you an authoritative ground truth. On Wednesday, you ran deterministic NLP pipelines like TreeTagger and SpaCy. You saw their speed, but you also saw them stumble on Out-of-Vocabulary historical spellings.

Today, we take Step 3 of our three-step cycle: AI models. In VS Code Antigravity, we can prompt AI models to analyze historical grammar.

Unlike deterministic taggers that follow rigid suffix rules, modern language models were trained on billions of words from historical book. Archives. They possess remarkable intuition for archaic vocabulary. However, they bring serious risks, including invented lemmas and unrequested modernizations. Today, you will test an AI model on your text, execute a three-way comparativ. Finalize your linguistic markup assignment.

Vocabulary. Language Model (LLM). An AI model trained on vast text datasets that predicts and generates natural language. Three-Way Comparative Audit — Comparing annotations across three tiers: manual human craft, deterministic NLP scrip. Generative ai models.

Takeaway: Large language models bring powerful intuition to historical language, but their outputs must be audited against manual ground truth.

name.text: 01 Question: The Friday Cycle: Benchmarking Generative AI Against Ground Truth

questiontext.text: What is the methodological goal of benchmarking generative AI and neural models against manual ground truth in Topic 8?

generalfeedback.text: The Friday cycle benchmarks neural transformers and LLMs against manual ground truth to quantify parsing precision, recall, and hallucination rates.

answer.text: To establish a rigorous evaluation harness that measures precision, recall, and F1 scores, identifying the boundaries between neural reasoning and morphological hallucination.

feedback.text: Correct. The objective is to quantify model performance objectively against the manual gold standard, exposing exact strengths and error modes.

answer.text: To prove that human philologists are unnecessary and can be replaced immediately by unmonitored chatbots.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human philological ground truth is the indispensable benchmark that makes evaluation possible.

answer.text: To train AI models to generate entirely fictitious historical manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital philology focuses on accurate representation and analysis of authentic historical texts.

answer.text: To eliminate all computational evaluation metrics in favor of subjective impressions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The lab builds a quantitative benchmarking harness based on mathematical precision, recall, and F1 metrics.

name.text: 02 Content: How Large Language Models Understand Historical Prose

questiontext.text:
How Large Language Models Understand Historical Prose

How can an AI model read eighteenth-century French or archaic legal Eng. A rule-based tool failed? The secret lies in pre-training data.

Deterministic taggers like TreeTagger rely on relatively small, modern dictionaries. If a word like décrétoit is missing from its dictionary, the tool fails. By contrast, AI models have ingested millions of digitized historical books, including eighteenth-century F. Colonial treaties.

During training, the model learned statistical associations across centuries of language change. It knows that eighteenth-century French authors wrote -oit where modern writers use -ait. It knows that shew'd means showed. This broad historical exposure gives neural models a significant advantage over simple lookup. Reading archival prose.

Vocabulary. Pre-Training Data — The massive collection of digital book. Historical documents used to train a neural language model. Context Window — The amount of surrounding text a model considers when analyzing words.

Takeaway: Language models succeed on historical prose because their training data includes centuries of digitized historical literature.

name.text: 02 Question: Neural Architectures in Classical Philology: From RNNs to Transformers

questiontext.text: Why are transformer self-attention mechanisms superior to recurrent neural networks (RNNs/Bi-LSTMs) for parsing classical historical languages?

generalfeedback.text: Transformer self-attention mechanisms resolve long-distance hyperbaton by computing direct dependencies between words across entire sentences simultaneously.

answer.text: Self-attention computes direct dependency scores between all word pairs simultaneously across the entire sentence, easily resolving long-distance hyperbaton.

feedback.text: Correct. Transformers compute token compatibility in parallel regardless of linear distance, avoiding the gradient degradation that causes RNNs to lose long-distance dependencies.

answer.text: Transformers process only one single character at a time and ignore sentence context.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transformers process whole sentences simultaneously with full bidirectional context.

answer.text: RNNs are too fast and accurate for historical research purposes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RNNs struggle with long-distance syntactic dependencies in languages with flexible word order.

answer.text: Transformers do not require any electricity or computing hardware to run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transformers require matrix multiplication hardware (CPUs/GPUs); their advantage is architectural attention modeling.

name.text: 03 Content: Structured Prompt Engineering for Linguistic Markup

questiontext.text:
Structured Prompt Engineering for Linguistic Markup

While an AI model understands historical vocabulary, it will not output TEI XML automatically unless you instruct it with care. In computational editing, we use structured prompt engineering.

A structured prompt gives the model three essential things:

  1. Role Definition: Instruct the model to act as an expert computational philologist and TEI encoder.
  2. Task Specification: Instruct the model to tokenize the passage, look up canonical lemmas, and assign Universal Dependencies tags.
  3. Output Format: Explicitly demand valid TEI P5 XML wrapped in <s>, <w>, and <pc> elements.

Without strict prompt formatting, models tend to produce conversational essays or unformatted markdown tables. A structured prompt forces the model to return clean, machine-readable XML.

Vocabulary. System Prompt — High-level instructions provided to an AI model that define its p. Required output format. Structured Output — Machine-readable output (such as valid XML or JSON) constrained by strict formatting rules.

Takeaway: Structured prompts define the model's expert role, specify its linguistic task, and enforce strict TEI XML output formatting.

name.text: 03 Question: Specialized Neural Encoders: GreBERTa and PhilBERTa

questiontext.text: How do specialized neural encoders like GreBERTa and PhilBERTa achieve high-accuracy, deterministic morphological tagging?

generalfeedback.text: Specialized neural encoders like GreBERTa leverage bidirectional masked pre-training on classical corpora to deliver highly accurate, deterministic morphological classification.

answer.text: They utilize bidirectional transformer encoders pre-trained on classical Greek/Latin corpora and fine-tuned on dependency treebanks to classify tokens from fixed tagsets.

feedback.text: Correct. By training on historical corpora (TLG, Perseus) and fine-tuning on treebanks (AGLDT, PROIEL), encoder models predict UPOS and FEATS without generative hallucinations.

answer.text: They translate ancient texts into modern French before looking up English dictionary definitions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GreBERTa and PhilBERTa operate directly on ancient Greek and Latin token embeddings.

answer.text: They generate random text completions by sampling from modern social media posts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These models are encoder-only classifiers trained on curated historical literary corpora.

answer.text: They delete all inflected endings and replace them with modern punctuation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They perform token classification to assign standard UPOS and morphological feature tags.

name.text: 04 Content: Providing the Universal Dependencies Schema in Prompts

questiontext.text:
Providing the Universal Dependencies Schema in Prompts

Never assume an AI model remembers the exact tags you want. Large models know dozens of different grammar tagsets, from older Penn Treebank tags to French national standards.

To guarantee consistent output, provide the exact Universal Dependencies (UD) tagset directly in your prompt. List the core UPOS tags: NOUN, VERB, ADJ, ADV, PRON, DET, AUX, ADP, CCONJ,. punct.

Instruct the model explicitly: Use only official Universal Dependencies UPOS tags in the pos attribute. When the model has the allowed tags in its prompt, it will not invent non-standard labels like PREP or ARTICLE. This keeps the AI output aligned with your Tuesday ground truth and Wednesday NLP benchmark.

Takeaway: Including the 17 Universal Dependencies UPOS tags in your prompt prevents the model from inventing non-standard grammatical labels.

name.text: 04 Question: Sequence-to-Sequence String Transduction: GreTA and PhilTA

questiontext.text: How do sequence-to-sequence models like GreTA and PhilTA solve the lemmatization of irregular and suppletive verbs?

generalfeedback.text: Sequence-to-sequence transformers like GreTA treat lemmatization as contextual string transduction, decoding canonical dictionary headwords character by character.

answer.text: They formulate lemmatization as contextual string transduction, decoding canonical dictionary headwords character by character from bidirectional sentence embeddings.

feedback.text: Correct. GreTA uses a T5 encoder-decoder architecture to generate lemmas dynamically at the character level, handling irregular principal parts and ablaut without intermediate POS bottlenecks.

answer.text: They search an unchangeable static lookup table and fail whenever an irregular verb is encountered.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sequence-to-sequence decoders generate character sequences dynamically, generalizing beyond static tables.

answer.text: They assign every verb the generic lemma 'verbum'.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GreTA generates precise dictionary headwords (e.g. mapping ἦλθον to ἔρχομαι).

answer.text: They require human users to type the lemma before they can output the sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. GreTA is fully automated and infers lemmas directly from sentence context.

name.text: 05 Content: Enforcing Strict Negative Constraints

questiontext.text:
Enforcing Strict Negative Constraints

In prompt engineering, what you forbid is just as important as what you request. These boundaries are called negative constraints.

Language models are trained to be helpful assistants. When they see historical spelling mistakes or scribal abbreviations, their default instinct is to "fix" the text for modern readers. In scholarly editing, this instinct corrupts historical evidence!

Include these four negative constraints in your prompt:

  1. DO NOT alter surface text: Preserve the exact historical characters, spelling slips, and accents inside the <w> tags.
  2. DO NOT invent lemmas: Use modern canonical dictionary headwords; do not invent archaic lemmas like faisoir.
  3. DO NOT drop punctuation: Enclose every comma, period, and colon in a <pc> tag.
  4. DO NOT wrap in markdown fences: Output raw XML without conversational introductions or explanations.

Negative constraints rein in the model's helpful impulses and enforce scholarly discipline.

Vocabulary. Negative Constraint. An explicit instruction in a prompt that forbids unwanted model behaviors, such as modernizing spelling or dropping punctuation.

Takeaway: Negative constraints prevent AI models from modernizing historical spellings, dropping punctuation, or adding conversational filler.

name.text: 05 Question: State-of-the-Art Latin Parsing: The Cracovia System

questiontext.text: What dual-head architecture enabled the Cracovia system to achieve the top performance (F1 = 0.9627) in the EvaLatin 2022 competition?

generalfeedback.text: The Cracovia system combines XLM-RoBERTa encoders with multi-task fine-tuning on LASLA and UD treebanks to achieve state-of-the-art Latin morphological tagging.

answer.text: It fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa with shared representations across two specialized heads: one for coarse UPOS and one for fine-grained FEATS morphosyntactic bundles.

feedback.text: Correct. The Cracovia system shares transformer representations across joint UPOS and FEATS prediction heads, learning mutual grammatical constraints across the LASLA and UD treebanks.

answer.text: It disabled all neural network layers and relied exclusively on a 19th-century printed dictionary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cracovia is a state-of-the-art transformer architecture built upon cross-lingual XLM-RoBERTa encoders.

answer.text: It restricted Latin parsing to simple three-word sentences from elementary school textbooks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cracovia was benchmarked on complex classical Latin prose and poetry across 1.7 million LASLA tokens.

answer.text: It replaced Latin case categories with modern English word-order rules.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cracovia explicitly models Latin nominal cases, verbal moods, and agreement features.

name.text: 06 Content: Invented word Modes in Historical Lemmatization

questiontext.text:
Invented word Modes in Historical Lemmatization

The greatest danger when using AI in scholarly editing is invented word. A inv. A model generates plausible-sounding output that is factually wrong or non-existent.

In linguistic markup, invented words take specific forms:

  • Invented Lemmas: The model invents a fake Latin or Old French root word that never existed in any dictionary.
  • Confabulated Meanings: The model invents an imaginary historical meaning to explain an unusual spelling.
  • Ghost Morphemes: The model breaks a simple word into non-existent prefixes and suffixes.

Because language models write with total grammatical confidence, invented words can easily fool unwary editors. Every lemma produced by an AI model must be checked against an authoritative dictionary (OED or TLFi).

Vocabulary. Invented word — Confidently generated model output that is factually false, ungrounded, or non-existent in reality. Lexical Verification — Checking model-generated words against an authoritative reference dictionary.

Takeaway: AI models can confidently invent non-existent lemmas; every AI-generated headword must be verified against an authoritative lexicon.

name.text: 06 Question: Generalized Large Language Models in Morphological Analysis

questiontext.text: How do generalized Large Language Models (LLMs) differ fundamentally from dedicated neural parsers like GreBERTa or Cracovia?

generalfeedback.text: General-purpose LLMs possess broad emergent philological reasoning, but their probabilistic sampling creates non-deterministic outputs that require systematic validation.

answer.text: LLMs rely on in-context learning and autoregressive token sampling from massive multilingual pre-training rather than fixed tag classification over formal grammar rules.

feedback.text: Correct. LLMs generate text probabilistically from broad pre-training weights, exhibiting emergent philological reasoning but introducing potential formatting drift and hallucination risks.

answer.text: LLMs can only process numbers and cannot understand text or language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs excel at linguistic and semantic tasks due to extensive pre-training.

answer.text: Dedicated parsers generate conversational explanations, while LLMs output only binary machine code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs produce natural language explanations; dedicated parsers output structured tagsets.

answer.text: There are no differences; LLMs and dedicated parsers use identical software and training datasets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dedicated parsers are task-specific discriminative models; LLMs are massive generative autoregressive models.

name.text: 07 Content: The Modernizing error Hazard in Historical Linguistics

questiontext.text:
The Modernizing error Hazard in Historical Linguistics

A subtle form of invented word is modernizing error. Modernizing. A model treats a genuine historical feature as an error and silently "corrects" it.

In Andromeda's 1752 Treaty, the scribe wrote acknowledg'd. An AI model might silently change the surface text to acknowledged inside the <w> tag, erasing the historical apostrophe. In Maud Lewis's letters, an informal phrase like them things might be silently converted to those things.

In Ace's 1791 decree, an 18th-century verb form like décrétoit might be silently changed to décrétait. When an editor asks for linguistic markup, they want tags attached to the historical ink, not a modern rewrite. Tracking modernizing errors is one of your main tasks during today's audit.

Vocabulary. Modernizing error — An autom. A model inappropriately modernizes or standardizes genuine historical language features.

Takeaway: Watch out for hypercorrection: AI models often try to smooth away historical spellings, contractions, and scribal quirks.

name.text: 07 Question: The Precision-Recall Paradox in LLM POS Tagging

questiontext.text: What characterizes the 'Precision-Recall Paradox' observed when evaluating zero-shot LLMs on Latin and Greek POS tagging?

generalfeedback.text: LLMs exhibit near-perfect precision but poor recall in zero-shot POS tagging, frequently skipping or dropping ambiguous historical tokens.

answer.text: LLMs achieve near-perfect precision (>99%) when asserting tags, but suffer low recall (<89%) because they frequently drop or skip ambiguous tokens.

feedback.text: Correct. Zero-shot LLMs are highly conservative: their predictions are almost always accurate, but they omit difficult or ambiguous historical tokens, reducing overall F1 below dedicated taggers.

answer.text: LLMs achieve 100% recall on all words but have 0% precision on common nouns.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The paradox is high precision paired with lower recall due to token dropping.

answer.text: LLMs execute tag predictions faster than dedicated C-based tools like TreeTagger.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLM inference is substantially slower and more computationally intensive than local taggers.

answer.text: LLMs produce identical precision and recall scores regardless of prompt design.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompt engineering and few-shot exemplars significantly alter LLM recall and precision balances.

name.text: 08 Content: Handling Out-of-Vocabulary Terms with Generative Context

questiontext.text:
Handling Out-of-Vocabulary Terms with Generative Context

While AI models have risks, they also possess genuine strengths. Their greatest advantage over deterministic taggers is their ability to handle Out-of-Vocabulary historical words.

On Wednesday, you saw that TreeTagger failed on décrétoit. shew'd because those exact spellings were missing from its modern dictionary. A AI model does not suffer from this rigid limitation.

Because the AI model reads the entire sentence, it understands the syntax. It sees that décrétoit occupies the finite verb slot following the subject l'Assemblée. It recognizes the historical -oit suffix as an older imperfect ending. It correctly deduces that the base lemma is décréter. Where deterministic tools fail, generative models use context to solve historical puzzles.

Takeaway: Generative AI models use full sentence context to deduce correct lemmas for historical spellings that break deterministic taggers.

name.text: 08 Question: Zero-Shot vs. Few-Shot In-Context Prompting

questiontext.text: Why does providing few-shot annotated exemplars in an LLM prompt improve morphological tagging performance?

generalfeedback.text: Few-shot prompting with annotated exemplars anchors LLM output to standard tagsets, dramatically improving recall and citation consistency.

answer.text: Exemplars anchor the model's output distribution, enforcing strict tagset vocabularies, boosting recall on closed-class words, and standardizing dictionary citation forms.

feedback.text: Correct. Few-shot demonstrations constrain the LLM to valid UD tags, prevent invented labels, recover missing particles, and ensure adherence to canonical LSJ/OLD lemma conventions.

answer.text: Exemplars permanently retrain the base weights of the remote cloud model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. In-context learning conditions the active inference context; it does not update base model weights.

answer.text: Exemplars reduce prompt length and make the API call free of charge.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adding exemplars increases prompt token count and API cost, but significantly improves accuracy and tagset compliance.

answer.text: Exemplars force the model to respond exclusively in Latin poetry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Exemplars guide the model to output structured JSON or CoNLL-U annotations.

name.text: 09 Content: Prompting for TEI XML vs JSON Output

questiontext.text:
Prompting for TEI XML vs JSON Output

When designing an AI pipeline, you have two choices for output format: requesting raw TEI XML directly, or requesting structured JSON that you convert to XML with a script.

Requesting TEI XML directly is fast and convenient:

<w lemma="promise" pos="VERB">promis'd</w>

However, models sometimes make small XML syntax errors, such as forgetting a closing tag or omitting quotes around attributes.

Requesting structured JSON is often more robust:

{"token": "promis'd", "lemma": "promise", "pos": "VERB"}

A short Python script can validate the JSON and convert it into valid TEI XML. For today's classroom exercise, prompting directly for clean TEI XML is completely f. Large projects often use the json-to-xml route.

Takeaway: Prompting for TEI XML directly is fast for short excerpts; prompting for JSON provides stricter programmatic validation for large texts.

name.text: 09 Question: Morphological Hallucination: Mechanisms and Manifestations

questiontext.text: What are the primary drivers of morphological hallucination when LLMs parse ancient historical languages?

generalfeedback.text: Morphological hallucination stems from modern language pre-training bias and analogical regularization of irregular historical paradigms.

answer.text: Modern language intrusion from pre-training data, false analogical regularization of suppletive verbs, and etymological over-decomposition.

feedback.text: Correct. Hallucination occurs when modern Greek/Romance data overrides ancient forms, when irregular suppletive roots are falsely regularized, or when rare compounds are split fictitiously.

answer.text: Hardware overheating causing random bit-flips in GPU memory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hallucination is a systemic linguistic phenomenon caused by training bias and analogical over-generalization.

answer.text: The total absence of ancient Greek and Latin texts on the internet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Classical texts are widely digitized; the issue is the overwhelming statistical preponderance of modern language data.

answer.text: Strict adherence to 19th-century German philological dictionaries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adherence to authoritative dictionaries prevents hallucinations rather than causing them.

name.text: 10 Content: The Three-Way Comparative Audit: Manual vs NLP vs AI

questiontext.text:
The Three-Way Comparative Audit: Manual vs NLP vs AI

Now we bring all three stages of Week Eight together in our Three-Way Comparative Audit.

Open three files side by side in VS Code:

  1. ground_truth_manual.xml: Tuesday's hand-verified philological baseline.
  2. nlp_baseline.xml: Wednesday's deterministic SpaCy / TreeTagger output.
  3. ground_truth_ai.xml: Today's AI-generated markup.

By comparing all three tiers across the exact same twenty-word passage, you can evaluate each technology objectively. Where did all three agree? Where did the deterministic tool fail while the AI succeeded? Where did the AI hallucinate while human scholarship stood firm?

Takeaway: The three-way audit compares manual, deterministic, and AI markup side by side, evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of each tier.

name.text: 10 Question: Comparative Benchmarks Across Classical Corpora

questiontext.text: According to comparative empirical benchmarks, which parsing architecture is most effective on standardized Classical Attic prose?

generalfeedback.text: Specialized taggers dominate standardized classical prose, while sequence-to-sequence models and LLMs excel on archaic poetry and noisy medieval manuscripts.

answer.text: Fine-tuned neural encoders (Cracovia) and large-lexicon probabilistic models (TreeTagger/Diorisis), which achieve over 96% accuracy at minimal computational cost.

feedback.text: Correct. Standardized prose is parsed near-flawlessly by specialized classical models, making expensive generative LLM inference unnecessary for standard texts.

answer.text: Zero-shot chatbots querying unconstrained consumer web interfaces.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unconstrained chatbots have lower recall and higher latency compared to dedicated classical parsers on standard prose.

answer.text: Manual transcription using physical typewriters without digital storage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital pipelines achieve massive throughput speed and high accuracy on standard corpora.

answer.text: Random guessing based on word length.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Structured linguistic models achieve >96% accuracy through formal grammar rules and trained embeddings.

name.text: 11 Content: Taxonomy of Discrepancies: Four Error Categories

questiontext.text:
Taxonomy of Discrepancies: Four Error Categories

When you compare your three files, you will find differences. To analyze them rigorously, classify every discrepancy into one of four standard categories:

Category Name Description and Cause Example
Category A Human Slip A human error in Tuesday's manual ground truth caused by fatigue or a typo. Human miskeyed lemma as trety
Category B Deterministic Rigid Miss The rule-based NLP tool failed due to an Out-of-Vocabulary historical spelling. SpaCy failed on décrétoit or shew'd
Category C AI Hallucination / Smoothing The AI model modernized spelling, invented a fake lemma, or dropped punctuation. AI altered promis'd to promised
Category D Genuine Crux / Ambiguity The text allows two equally valid grammatical readings; both tiers are defensible. Homograph will as noun vs auxiliary

This taxonomy turns random errors into structured scholarly insights.

Vocabulary. Error Taxonomy. A formal classification system used to categoriz. Analyze the root causes of computational and human errors.

Takeaway: Classify every disagreement into Category A (human slip), B (NLP rigid miss), C (AI hallucination), or D (genuine crux).

name.text: 11 Question: The Stress Test: Byzantine Epigrams and Unstandardized Orthography

questiontext.text: Why did state-of-the-art classical NLP pipelines suffer a 20–25% accuracy collapse when tested on the Database of Byzantine Book Epigrams (DBBE)?

generalfeedback.text: Unstandardized medieval manuscript transcriptions cause specialized classical taggers to suffer a catastrophic 20–25% accuracy collapse.

answer.text: The models were trained on standardized classical texts and failed when confronted with unedited scribal transcriptions containing pervasive itacism and phonetic spellings.

feedback.text: Correct. Pre-trained models expect normalized classical orthography; unedited manuscript transcriptions with itacisms cause out-of-vocabulary lookup misses and subword fragmentation.

answer.text: Byzantine book epigrams were written in an unknown non-human language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The poems are in medieval Greek; the challenge is unstandardized scribal orthography.

answer.text: The DBBE database corrupted the text files with computer viruses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. DBBE is a prestigious academic corpus of authentic medieval manuscript transcriptions.

answer.text: Treebanks are legally prohibited from parsing Byzantine literature.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The collapse is purely algorithmic: classical models fail to generalize to noisy medieval scribal spelling.

name.text: 12 Content: Evaluating Token-Level Accuracy Across All Three Tiers

questiontext.text:
Evaluating Token-Level Accuracy Across All Three Tiers

To complete your benchmark, calculate token-level accuracy for both automated tiers against your manual ground truth.

Create a summary comparison table in your notes:

Metric Deterministic NLP (SpaCy / TreeTagger) AI Model (Antigravity / Claude)
Total Tokens Evaluated 20 20
Matching UPOS Tags 18 / 20 (90%) 19 / 20 (95%)
Matching Lemmas 16 / 20 (80%) 19 / 20 (95%)
Overall Token Accuracy 80% 95%

In most historical documents, the AI model scores higher on lemm. Of its broader vocabulary. It may lose points on punctuation or surface-text alterations.

Takeaway: Calculate token-level POS and Lemma accuracy for both automated tiers to see which tool performed best on your document.

name.text: 12 Question: Linguistic Noise 1: Itacism and Vowel Mergers

questiontext.text: How does itacistic vowel merger (e.g. scribes writing γινώσκω or γεινώσκω for γιγνώσκω) disrupt transformer-based language models?

generalfeedback.text: Itacism merges six distinct historical vowel spellings into the [i] sound, causing catastrophic lexicon lookup misses and transformer subword fragmentation.

answer.text: It causes subword tokenizers to fragment unfamiliar phonetic spellings into arbitrary subword units, corrupting contextual embeddings and causing lexicon lookup misses.

feedback.text: Correct. Non-standard vowel spellings break subword tokenization (creating fragments like ['##οτ', '##ήσ', '##θι']), destroying the root's semantic representation.

answer.text: It forces the model to shut down and delete the operating system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Itacism degrades linguistic accuracy; it does not affect operating system integrity.

answer.text: It makes the transformer believe that all words are Latin adjectives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The issue is subword fragmentation and lexical mismatch, leading to false POS and lemma predictions.

answer.text: It has zero effect because transformer models ignore vowels entirely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transformers process subword tokens derived directly from character strings, making them sensitive to spelling shifts.

name.text: 13 Content: Calculating AI Precision, Recall, and Invented word Rates

questiontext.text:
Calculating AI Precision, Recall, and Invented word Rates

In addition to accuracy, calculate the model's invented word rate and modernizing error rate.

Use these two simple metrics:

  • Hallucination Rate: (Number of Invented Lemmas / Total Tokens) * 100. In a sound scholarly prompt, this should be 0%.
  • Hypercorrection Rate: (Number of Altered Surface Words / Total Tokens) * 100. This measures how often the model modernized your historical characters.

If the model changed promis'd to promised once in twenty words, its modernizing error rate is 5%. Documenting these rates proves that you are evaluating AI with scientific rigor.

Takeaway: Quantify AI risks by calculating hallucination and hypercorrection rates alongside standard precision and recall scores.

name.text: 13 Question: Linguistic Noise 2: Omission of Iota Subscript and Diacritics

questiontext.text: Why is the omission of the iota subscript in manuscript transcriptions a critical vector of grammatical error?

generalfeedback.text: Omission of the iota subscript obliterates the morphological boundary between datives, nominatives, subjunctives, and adverbs.

answer.text: It removes the overt graphemic distinction between dative singular nouns and nominative nouns, as well as between subjunctive and indicative verbs.

feedback.text: Correct. Without the subscript iota, dative forms (καρδίᾳ) become identical to nominatives (καρδία), causing automated parsers to systematically misassign case and mood.

answer.text: It prevents the text from being rendered in digital fonts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unicode renders text with or without diacritics; the error is grammatical disambiguation.

answer.text: It changes all Greek verbs into indeclinable prepositions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Verbs remain verbs, but mood distinctions (subjunctive vs. indicative) are obscured.

answer.text: It only affects modern 21st-century texts, never medieval manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omitting the silent iota subscript was standard practice among medieval scribes.

name.text: 14 Content: Testing AI on Andromeda's 1752 Treaty Excerpt

questiontext.text:
Testing AI on Andromeda's 1752 Treaty Excerpt

Let us look at how an AI model performs on Andromeda's project: the 1752 P. Friendship treaty.

Clause: All Treaties shall be renewed by the Governor.

Here is the three-way comparison:

  • Manual Ground Truth: All (DET, all), Treaties (NOUN, treaty), shall (AUX, shall), be (AUX, be), renewed (VERB, renew).
  • Deterministic SpaCy: Matched all five tokens perfectly (100% accuracy).
  • AI Model: Matched all five tokens perfectly, and correctly identified that renewed is a passive participle.

On standard 18th-century legal formulas, both automated tools perform exceptionally well. Disagreements only emerge when archaic contractions like promis'd or legal compounds like whereunto appear.

Takeaway: On standard legal English formulas, both deterministic NLP and AI models achieve near-perfect agreement with human ground truth.

name.text: 14 Question: Linguistic Noise 3: Uncontracted Dialectal Forms and Archaic Suffixes

questiontext.text: How does Homeric dialectal morphology challenge NLP models trained primarily on Classical Attic prose?

generalfeedback.text: Uncontracted vowels, archaic suffixes, and unaugmented verbs in Homeric Greek cause Attic-trained taggers to misclassify tense, aspect, and nominal case.

answer.text: Archaic uncontracted vowels (στήθεα), epic case suffixes (-οιο, -φι), and unaugmented verbs (βάλε) violate Attic rules, causing high out-of-vocabulary rates and misclassified tenses.

feedback.text: Correct. Attic models fail on Homeric dialectal variants, frequently misparsing uncontracted substantives as proper names and unaugmented past verbs as imperatives.

answer.text: Homeric Greek contains no nouns or pronouns.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Homeric Greek has a rich nominal system with distinctive archaic case endings.

answer.text: Attic prose models automatically translate Homeric epic into modern English verse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Classical Attic models attempt to parse Homeric forms against Attic rules, leading to errors.

answer.text: Homeric poetry was composed without vowels.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Homeric Greek is fully vocalic and metrically structured in dactylic hexameter.

name.text: 15 Content: Testing AI on Ace's 1791 French Decree Excerpt

questiontext.text:
Testing AI on Ace's 1791 French Decree Excerpt

Now let us examine Ace's project: a 1791 French Revolutionary decree containing the archaic verb décrétoit.

Sentence: L'Assemblée nationale décrétoit la loi.

Here is the three-way comparison:

  • Manual Ground Truth: décrétoit → lemma décréter, UPOS VERB, Features: Tense=Imp|VerbForm=Fin.
  • Deterministic SpaCy: décrétoit → lemma décrétoit, UPOS NOUN (Category B error: OOV suffix failure).
  • AI Model: décrétoit → lemma décréter, UPOS VERB, Features: Tense=Imp|VerbForm=Fin (Match!).

Look at that result! SpaCy failed because -oit was missing from its modern dictionary. The AI model recognized the 18th-century suffix. Mapped the verb to its proper infinitive décréter. This is a clear demonstration of AI's strength on historical morphology.

Takeaway: AI models successfully resolve 18th-century French verbal suffixes like -oit where deterministic dictionaries fail.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Joint learning explicitly shares encoder representations across complementary tasks.

Testing AI on Maud Lewis's Folk Correspondence Excerpt

name.text: 17 Content: Adjudicating Disagreements: The Editor as Arbiter

questiontext.text:
Adjudicating Disagreements: The Editor as Arbiter

After completing your three-way audit, you will have a table of disagreements. Now comes the core scholarly duty: editorial adjudication.

An algorithm cannot decide what belongs in your final edition. The human editor is the ultimate arbiter. Go through each discrepancy:

  • If the machine made an error (Category B or C), reject the machine prediction and keep your manual ground truth.
  • If the machine exposed a genuine human slip in your Tuesday table (Category A), gratefully correct your ground truth!
  • If the disagreement is a genuine crux (Category D), select the reading best supported by historical evidence and document your reasons.

This review process transforms raw machine output into reliable, peer-reviewed scholarship.

Vocabulary. Editorial Adjudication. The scholarly decision-making p. A human editor resolves conflicting readings and approves the final text.

Takeaway: The human editor serves as the ultimate arbiter, adjudicating every machine disagreement before publishing the edition.

name.text: 19 Content: Transparent Metadata Attribution with `@resp`

questiontext.text:
Transparent Metadata Attribution with `@resp`

In digital scholarly editions, transparency is paramount. R. Researchers must know who produced each annotation: a human scholar, a deterministic script, or an ai model.

TEI P5 provides the @resp (responsibility) attribute for this exact purpose. In your teiHeader, define your agents:

<respStmt>
  <resp>Manual annotation</resp>
  <name xml:id="editor">Ken Penner</name>
</respStmt>
<respStmt>
  <resp>Deterministic NLP pipeline</resp>
  <name xml:id="spacy">SpaCy 3.7 (en_core_web_sm)</name>
</respStmt>
<respStmt>
  <resp>AI-assisted parsing</resp>
  <name xml:id="claude">Claude 3.5 Sonnet / Antigravity</name>
</respStmt>

On your <w> elements, you can cite who verified the tag: <w lemma="renew" pos="VERB" resp="#editor">. Transparent attribution ensures full academic integrity.

Vocabulary. @resp. The tei attribute that indicates who is responsible for a specific editorial decision, correction, or markup layer.

Takeaway: Use the TEI @resp attribute and header statements to document whether annotations came from human editors, scripts, or AI models.

name.text: 20 Content: Combining All Layers: The Complete TEI Architecture

questiontext.text:
Combining All Layers: The Complete TEI Architecture

Take a moment to admire what your TEI document now contains. Over eight weeks, you have built a deeply layered digital monument:

  1. Metadata Layer: The teiHeader catalogues author, date, archive, license, and project policies.
  2. Image Layer: The <facsimile> container links high-resolution image manifests directly to text surfaces.
  3. Diplomatic Layer: The transcribed text preserves original ink, scribal lineation (<lb/>), and historical characters.
  4. Regularization Layer: The <choice> elements pair original spellings (<orig>) with modernized readings (<reg>).
  5. Linguistic Layer: The <w> and <s> elements record dictionary lemmas, parts of speech, and syntactic features.

All five layers coexist in a single well-formed XML file. This is the true power of the Text Encoding Initiative.

Takeaway: Your final TEI file unifies metadata, images, diplomatic text, normalized readings, and linguistic grammar in a single standards-compliant document.

name.text: 21 Content: Building Syntactic Dependency Trees with AI

questiontext.text:
Building Syntactic Dependency Trees with AI

In addition to parts of speech, you can prompt modern AI models to generate complete Universal Dependencies syntax trees in CoNLL-U format.

In your prompt, instruct the model: For each word, identify its governing head ID. Its deprel relation tag. The model will output the full 10-column table, identifying the root v. Linking subjects, obj. Modifiers.

When evaluating AI syntax trees, check for cycle errors. In a valid dependency tree, no word can depend on itself. Arrows must never form closed loops. The tree must form a clean hierarchy descending from the central root verb.

Vocabulary. Treebank — A text corpus annotated with complete syntactic dependency or phrase-structure trees. Cycle Error. An invalid syntactic grap. Dependency links form an infinite closed loop rather than a rooted tree.

Takeaway: AI models can predict complete syntactic dependency trees, but editors must audit them to ensure clean hierarchies without cycle errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The harness evaluates every token in the passage across all morphological dimensions.

name.text: 22 Content: Auditing AI Dependency Trees Against Ground Truth

questiontext.text:
Auditing AI Dependency Trees Against Ground Truth

Auditing a syntax tree is straightforward when you follow the grammatical flow of the sentence.

Ask these four structural questions:

  1. Root Check: Did the model assign root to the main finite verb or participle?
  2. Subject Check: Does the nominal subject (nsubj) point directly to the root verb?
  3. Object Check: Does the direct object (obj) attach to its governing transitive verb?
  4. Preposition Check: Do prepositions attach to their noun objects with relation case?

If the model attaches an adverbial clause to the wrong noun, correct the head ID. Auditing syntax trees sharpens your understanding of how historical authors constructed arguments.

Takeaway: Audit AI dependency trees by verifying root verbs, subject links, direct objects, and prepositional attachments.

name.text: 22 Question: Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and Macro-F1

questiontext.text: Why is Macro-averaged F1 more revealing than Micro-averaged accuracy when evaluating historical language taggers?

generalfeedback.text: Macro-averaged F1 weights rare and frequent grammatical categories equally, exposing model blind spots on sparse historical morphology.

answer.text: Macro-F1 assigns equal weight to rare and frequent categories, exposing model blind spots on sparse historical morphology (such as optatives or duals).

feedback.text: Correct. Micro-accuracy is dominated by high-frequency nouns and verbs; Macro-F1 weights all grammatical classes equally, preventing rare category failures from being masked.

answer.text: Macro-F1 can only be calculated on modern newspaper corpora.

name.text: 28 Content: Looking Ahead: From Words to Named Entities in Module 9

questiontext.text:
Looking Ahead: From Words to Named Entities in Module 9

Congratulations on completing Module 8! You have mastered grammatical words, dictionary headwords, and syntactic trees.

Next week, in Module 9, we take the next logical step in digital textual editing: Named Entity Recognition (NER).

Grammar tells us what a word does in a sentence (it is a noun, a verb, an adjective). Named entity markup tells us what a word refers to in the real world:

  • People: <persName> (Peregrine Thomas Hopson, Maud Lewis, King Louis XVI).
  • Places: <placeName> (Halifax, Nova Scotia, Paris).
  • Organizations: <orgName> (National Assembly, Mi'kmaq Nation).

Your linguistic markup provides the grammatical foundation on which named entity recognition will build.

Takeaway: Module 9 will build on your linguistic markup by identifying and encoding named people, places, and historical organizations.

name.text: 30 Content: Human Judgment in an Era of Linguistic AI

questiontext.text:
Human Judgment in an Era of Linguistic AI

As AI models grow more f. Capable, some people wonder if human textual scholarship will become obsolete.

Week Eight gives you the definitive answer to that question: absolutely not.

An AI model has no historical stake in truth. It will happily alter historical characters, smooth over scribal slip. Invent non-existent latin roots with absolute confidence. It cannot replace the scholar who spent months studying the ink, the pap. The archival context of an eighteenth-century document.

AI models are extraordinary power tools. But power tools require a skilled craftsperson. You are the craftsperson. Your historical knowledge, your philological judgment,. Your commitment to truth are what make digital editions trustworthy. Keep that critical human eye sharp, and enjoy your weekend!

Takeaway: AI provides extraordinary speed, but human scholars remain the essential guardians of historical truth and textual integrity.
